draft.title: Courts and statutory interpretation
card: Parliament writes Acts, but the words cannot cover every case. When a word or phrase in an Act is unclear, a court must decide what it means in the case before it.
This is statutory interpretation. The judge works out what the words mean, and does not rewrite the Act.
A court can read a word widely, so more situations are covered. It can read the word narrowly, so fewer situations are covered.
The meaning the court gives becomes part of the common law. It is a precedent that later courts may need to follow when the same words arise again.
draft.remember: Courts decide what unclear words in an Act mean, and that meaning can guide later cases.

a.q: A court is asked what an unclear word in an Act means. What is the court doing?
opts: Interpreting the Act to decide how it applies to the case
Repealing the word so that it no longer has any effect
Passing a new Act to replace the unclear wording
Asking parliament to vote on the meaning of the word
a.why: The court applies the Act to the case, so it must decide what the unclear word means. It cannot repeal or replace the Act, because that is a job for parliament.
a.clue: The court must still decide the case in front of it.

b.q: An Act bans 'vehicles' in Wattle Park. A Supreme Court judge rules that an electric scooter is not a vehicle, and so is allowed. What is the effect of this ruling?
opts: It narrows the word and may bind lower courts later
It widens the word and covers more things than before
It changes the Act, so parliament must now vote on it
It applies only to this scooter and to no later case
b.why: The judge read 'vehicles' so that it covers less, which narrows it. The meaning becomes precedent, so lower courts may have to follow it. Widening would mean scooters were caught by the ban.
b.clue: Did the ruling bring more things under the ban or fewer?

a.best: Interpreting the Act to decide how it applies to the case

b.best: It narrows the word and may bind lower courts later
